title: Housing affordability and homelessness, 19 days of posts

clusters.text: Activists applaud a psychotic homeless woman for choosing to live on the streets as an expression of bodily autonomy.
clusters.verdict_basis: I found no record or news report of a specific incident matching this claim. None showed activists praising a "psychotic" homeless woman for living on the streets as bodily autonomy, and none was tied to Texas. The claim names no person, place, date or group, so there is nothing concrete to check. The Texas coverage I found, from the Texas Tribune, is about camping-ban policy. It reports that [advocates argue camping bans don't address the underlying shortage of affordable housing](https://www.texastribune.org/?p=128561). That is a policy argument, not a celebration of someone choosing street life. A [psychiatric study of homeless psychotic women](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.2007.07071166) discusses why such women often refuse offers of help. It isn't about activists applauding anyone. The claim reads as a generalised characterisation, and it may refer to a specific viral post I couldn't find. I can't confirm or refute it.

clusters.text: In 2015, Los Angeles musician Elvis Summers built a tiny house for Smokie, a 60-year-old grandmother sleeping on the street.
clusters.verdict_basis: Contemporary reporting backs each element of the claim. The Christian Post (April 30, 2015), LAist and Global News/CBS say Elvis Summers, of South Los Angeles, built an 8-foot house on wheels for Irene "Smokie" McGhee. They describe her as a 60-year-old grandmother who had been homeless for about ten years and slept in the dirt on his street. The build and the viral video date to spring 2015, and the Christian Post story is dated April 2015. The "musician" label is also supported: Reason described him as a struggling South LA musician, and a later summary of his project says he started it. The claim is a few years old and is about California, not Texas, so it has no direct bearing on Texas policy. That doesn't change whether it is accurate. One minor wrinkle is that the Christian Post said Summers ran an online retail business, and one later CBS item gave the woman's age as 62. Most sources say 60, and the claim as worded is accurate.

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it

clusters.text: Elvis Summers raised over $100,000 to build 37 tiny houses for homeless people.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim matches 2016 reporting, though it isn't about Texas. Elvis Summers is a Los Angeles builder. 
NPR reported he had given out 37 tiny 6- by 8-foot houses, which cost $1,200 each to build.
 
Reason reported he raised over $100,000 through crowdfunding campaigns
, and 
Inside Edition said he raised over $100,000 through a GoFundMe campaign.
 There are two caveats. The main April 2016 GoFundMe appears to have 
raised $98,015 against a $100,000 goal
, so the "over $100,000" figure seems to be the total across campaigns. The count of 37 was also a snapshot from early 2016, and 
by September 2016 he said he was up to "41 or 42".
 The wording "to build 37" is therefore a fair but slightly loose summary.

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it

clusters.text: In 2016 the City of Los Angeles seized the tiny homes Elvis Summers built, and years later spent millions building its own tiny home villages.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Contemporary reporting confirms the 2016 seizures. KTLA (Feb 2016) reported that the city began seizing tiny houses Elvis Summers built and placed on South LA freeway overpasses. [Reason](https://reason.com/video/2016/12/09/los-angeles-homeless-tiny-houses/) said the City Council amended its sweeps ordinance so the houses could be taken without notice. The scale is smaller than "the tiny homes" suggests. Only about three were impounded at first, and Summers moved seven or eight others into storage before the city reached them. The [LA Times](https://www.pressreader.com/usa/los-angeles-times/20160423/281788513243109) reported in April 2016 that the city agreed to return the impounded houses to him.

The second half also checks out. [HUD USER](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/casestudies/study-092823.html) says the city built 10 tiny home villages as part of its 2021 COVID-era roadmap. That includes the Chandler Boulevard village at $4.9 million. The [A-Mark Foundation report](https://www.prweb.com/releases/new_report_estimates_costs_of_los_angeles_tiny_home_villages_intended_to_combat_homelessness/prweb18532499.htm) put construction costs at roughly $3 million to $9 million per villag

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it

clusters.text: Republicans have governed Texas for 30 years.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Republicans have held the governor's office continuously since George W. Bush took office on January 17, 1995, according to the 
Texas Legislative Reference Library's list of governors
. That is nearly 32 years, so "30 years" is a fair round number for the governorship. The rest of state government doesn't fit as well. 
Democrats won the lieutenant governor, attorney general and comptroller offices in 1994
, so they held those posts into the late 1990s. A Texas Scorecard timeline says 
the Senate flipped to Republicans in 1997 and the House in 2002
. That means full Republican control of the governor and both chambers is about 23–24 years old, not 30. The wording "governed … for 30 years" is accurate for the governor's office but overstates it for the Legislature, which writes the housing, zoning and homelessness laws the thread is about.

clusters.text: Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton are hypocritical for running on 'Fixing Texas' after decades of Republican control.
The poor condition of cheap hotel rooms is due to their low price, not to immigrants.
Developers should plant trees alongside new construction.
Social safety nets are failing in many areas of America because of the rapidly rising cost of living.
clusters.verdict_basis:
- Strain is real, but the cause is mixed. CPR (Colorado), Billy Penn (Philadelphia) and Capital B Atlanta report food banks under pressure. They blame 
cuts in federal food assistance and a rise in the cost of living
 together. CPBP data cited by Capital B shows 
national SNAP participation fell by 4 million from July 2025 to March 2026
 after the July 2025 federal law. So the claim's single cause, cost of living, leaves out a policy cause that the same reporting stresses.
- "Rapidly rising" is only partly right. BLS data reported by CNBC shows 
annual inflation of 3.7% in September
, which is up from 3.4% in August and driven largely by gasoline. Core CPI was 
2.6%
, and shelter inflation was 3.2% per Trading Economics. In Texas, the Texas Real Estate Research Center found 
statewide prices 0.2 percent below year-ago levels, with a median of $339,000, unchanged from last year
. Affordability is still poor. NLIHC reports 
only 26 rental homes affordable and available for every 100 extremely low-income households
, and the TAAHP survey found 
54% of Texans say housing affordability is getting worse in their community
. That is a high level of housing cost, not a sharp recent rise in

clusters.text: A mother of four was thrown out of a homeless shelter in Maricopa County despite her efforts.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim's wording matches the title of an MS NOW segment from "The Assignment with Antonia Hylton", which was posted around October 11, 2026. The segment 
features Marshae Jenkins, a mother of four who is getting help from AZ Hugs after she and her family were thrown out of a homeless shelter
. The segment's text says 
AZ Hugs founder Austin Davis helps families in Maricopa County
. A description of the segment says she is 
currently living in a motel in Arizona
. ProPublica's reporting from the same week shows the wider setting. 
Family homelessness in Maricopa County has risen to its highest level in more than a decade, while every shelter is full and housing vouchers are scarce.
 I found no record of the shelter's reason for removing her, and "despite her efforts" is the segment's framing of her own account. I could not check the underlying facts independently. Maricopa County is in Arizona, not Texas, so the claim is accurate as worded but has nothing to do with Texas policy. Some reposts also label the clip as NBC, but the original is MS NOW.

clusters.text: A robotic construction project in Texas is creating 121 homes for people who have experienced long-term homelessness.
clusters.verdict_basis:
ICON's own X post of Oct 9, 2026 said it is nearing completion of 121 homes at Austin's Community First! Village, which Mobile Loaves & Fishes runs for people with chronic homelessness. That is the source of the number, as relayed by 
Runtime Wire
. The same report notes that 
ICON's project page lists 117 structures at the site, built from 2019 through 2026
, and says the two totals shouldn't be treated as interchangeable. Designboom describes 
95 of a total 121 printed structures
, which counts "structures" rather than homes. ICON's 2024 announcement covered 
100 new 3D-printed homes
 on top of 
17 homes and facilities
 already built. The robotic, Texas and chronic-homelessness parts of the claim hold up. The "121 homes" figure comes from the company's own post, conflicts with its project page, and may include non-home structures. It also covers work since 2019, not a single project that is currently creating 121 homes. I found no independent count.

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it

clusters.text: The ICON robotic construction project in Texas is nearing completion.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim doesn't say which ICON project it means, and the answer changes by project. ICON's own project page lists 
Wolf Ranch in Georgetown, 100 structures, as finished in 2025
, and 
Designboom says ICON and Lennar completed the 100 houses in 2025
. The "nearing completion" wording matches a 
New Atlas article from August 14, 2024
, so it looks stale if Wolf Ranch is the target. The Fort Bliss barracks project was the other large Texas project I found. 
Stars and Stripes reported on July 28, 2026 that the first two of 10 buildings had opened, with the rest expected in September
. That project is probably complete or nearly so by mid-October, though I found no report confirming that. ICON's October 13, 2026 Series D coverage describes 
expansion across Texas and other markets
 and does not describe any single Texas project as nearing completion. I did not confirm the status of ICON's other Texas work, such as the Community First! Village homes, so I can't rule out that some project fits the claim.

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it

clusters.text: Foreign buyers are the reason homes are so expensive in America.
clusters.verdict_basis:
NAR's 2026 International Transactions report (published July 29, 2026) counts 
67,100 foreign-buyer purchases of existing homes between April 2025 and March 2026, the second-lowest level since NAR began tracking in 2009
. That is 
about 1.7% of existing-home purchases
. 
Most of those purchases (37,600, or 56%) were by recent immigrants or visa holders already living in the U.S.
, so buyers based abroad were fewer still. In Texas, 
12% of foreign purchasers bought there
, and the Texas Tribune's coverage of the comptroller's report describes 
a bipartisan consensus that affordability problems stem from a shortage of homes
. The Comptroller's report points to 
supply that hasn't kept up with demand
, 
higher interest rates
 and 
zoning and land-use rules that limit development
. Newsweek's reporting likewise says 
supply, construction levels, zoning and mortgage rates are much larger drivers of affordability than foreign ownership
. Foreign buyers can affect prices in some local markets, but a share this small does not support calling them "the reason" homes are expensive nationally. One caveat is that NAR's figures come from a member survey and may be imperfect.
